topic_title: Paper Stars Christmas Decor: 8 Ideas to Fold and Hang
intro: Paper stars cost very little and cover many jobs: a tree ornament, a gift tag, a garland, a window light or a wall display. Three choices decide how they turn out. Paper weight sets the shape, since cardstock holds points and printer paper curls. Folded stars take patience, while cut stars take minutes. Size sets the use: two inches for ornaments, six inches for windows and over 15 inches for lanterns. If you plan to make many, a star punch or template saves time, and a paper trimmer keeps strips even.

picks.description: The Froebel star is woven from four paper strips and ends up with eight points and a slight three-dimensional shape. It ranks first because it needs only strips, no glue and no scissors once the paper is cut. Use strips about 15 times as long as they are wide; a strip one inch wide and 15 inches long gives a star around three inches across. Fold, weave and tuck the ends, then pull the folds tight so the points sit evenly. The first star takes about 15 minutes, and later ones go faster. Because the star is flat enough to post in a card, it suits gift tags as well as tree ornaments. Double-sided origami strips make the pattern look striped, which gives a more finished result than plain paper. Rushing the tuck is the usual error.
picks.best_for: Crafters who like a puzzle and want an ornament they can make without glue
picks.skip_if: You want a quick project for a group, since the weaving steps frustrate young children
picks.quirky_fact: The Froebel star is named after Friedrich Froebel, the German educator who invented kindergarten.
picks.product_name: Origami Paper Strips Double Sided Assorted Colors

picks.description: A star lantern is a large hollow paper star with a small light inside, and it makes the biggest visual impact on this list. Pre-cut kits give 25 points and fold together with glue or slotted tabs, ending up about 15 to 25 inches across, so they suit a stairwell, porch or a high ceiling. Hang one from a hook with a cord, and put a battery LED light inside, never a bulb that produces heat or a real candle, because paper burns. Paper lanterns also fold flat for storage, so they last for years if kept dry. Assembly takes an hour or more for a first lantern, because the 25 points must meet cleanly, so allow an evening. The design is often linked to the Moravian star, said to have started in a German boys' school in the 1830s.
picks.best_for: Entryways and stairwells that need one large hanging light
picks.skip_if: You have a low ceiling or small space, since a 20 inch star crowds a small room
picks.quirky_fact: The classic Moravian star has 26 points, made up of 18 square and 8 triangular ones.
picks.product_name: Warm White LED Battery Tea Lights

picks.description: The woven star is the simplest paper star to make with children. Two strips are folded and interlocked to form a four-pointed shape that holds together without glue. It takes about five minutes once you know the fold, which makes it the fastest star here. Construction paper works well because it is stiff and the weave stays tight, while thin printer paper goes limp. Use strips about one inch wide and nine inches long for ornaments, or double the size for window stars. Younger children can manage this from about age eight with a demonstration, and younger ones can help by choosing colors. Make a batch of 30 in an afternoon and thread them on string to fill a window or a mantel. They are flat, so they pack into a shoebox and hold their shape for years.
picks.best_for: Families and classrooms who want a quick star that children can make themselves
picks.skip_if: You want a dimensional ornament, since this star is flat and small
picks.quirky_fact: Two strips of paper are enough for a star, so one sheet of construction paper makes about six.

picks.description: A star garland uses many small flat stars strung on a line, and it fills a mantel, shelf or banister more cheaply than a bought garland. Cut stars from cardstock with a star punch or a template, about two to three inches wide, then glue or tape each one to a length of twine at even gaps of four to six inches. A six foot garland needs about 15 stars. Use jute twine for a rustic look or white string for a lighter one, and choose cardstock over printer paper, which curls. Mix two sizes for rhythm. Hang the garland across a window or along a mantel with removable adhesive hooks. Because the stars are flat, the garland folds into a flat envelope for storage, which keeps the edges from creasing between seasons.
picks.best_for: Mantels, banisters and shelves that need a long, light line of decor
picks.skip_if: You want a garland that hangs from a high ceiling, since thin stars twist without weight
picks.quirky_fact: A star punch gives identical stars every time, which keeps a long garland looking even.

picks.description: Brown kraft stars bring a plain, natural look that sits well with evergreen, wood and dried orange slices. Trace a star template on kraft cardstock, cut it out, punch a hole at one tip and thread a short length of twine through it. Stamp or write a name, a date or a short message on each star with a white gel pen for a personal touch. At four inches wide, they work as gift tags as well as tree ornaments. Kraft cardstock is thick enough to hold its shape and takes ink without bleeding. Seal with a light coat of clear spray if you want them to last longer outdoors in sheltered places, since paper absorbs damp. Store them flat in a tin or box between layers of tissue so the points do not bend.
picks.best_for: Rustic or minimal trees and personalized gift tags
picks.skip_if: You want bright, shiny color, since kraft reads muted and plain
picks.quirky_fact: Kraft paper gets its brown color from unbleached wood pulp, which is why it is so strong.

picks.description: Window stars use translucent paper, and they glow when daylight passes through the glass, which looks like stained glass. The traditional German version uses kite paper, folded from squares, and glued with a small dab at each point. Cut or fold stars about four to six inches wide, then tape them to the window with the glossy side facing out. Layering two colors creates a third where they overlap. They look best on windows that face the street, because they are seen from outside after dark if a lamp is on inside. Transparent paper is thin, so handle it carefully and cut it with sharp scissors. Window stars fade in direct summer sun, but December light is weak enough that they last the season. Take them down gently and store flat between sheets of parchment.
picks.best_for: Street-facing windows and rooms with plenty of daylight
picks.skip_if: Your window faces away from daylight, since the effect needs light behind the paper
picks.quirky_fact: Window stars of translucent paper are a long-running Christmas tradition in Germany.
picks.product_name: Transparent Window Color Paper Assorted Sheets

picks.description: A handmade star for the top of the tree uses heavy glitter cardstock cut into two matching stars, then glued back to back around a cardboard tube or a bamboo skewer. It costs a fraction of a bought topper and can match the colors of the tree exactly. Cut a five-point star about eight inches across from two sheets, score the center fold, and glue them together with a hot glue gun or strong craft glue. For a three-dimensional look, make four stars and join them along a center fold. Slide the finished topper onto the top branch and check it sits straight. Glitter sheds, so seal the surface with a thin coat of clear glue if you do not want the sparkle on the carpet. A paper topper is light, which suits small trees that cannot hold a heavy glass one.
picks.best_for: Small trees and tabletop trees that need a light topper
picks.skip_if: You have a large tree, since a paper star looks small and light on a six foot tree
picks.quirky_fact: A topper this light can sit on trees that would bend under a glass finial.

picks.description: A cluster of stars in several sizes on a wall creates a Christmas tree shape or a loose constellation without any tree at all, which suits small rooms and rentals. Cut stars from one to eight inches wide in white, gold and kraft paper, then arrange them on the floor first to plan the layout. Fix each one to the wall with mounting putty, which comes off without damaging paint when handled gently. Start with the largest star near the center, then build outward, leaving uneven gaps. A cluster of around 20 stars fills a wall about three feet wide. Keep colors to two or three shades so it reads as designed, not busy. When the season ends, peel the putty and store the stars in a flat folder. They can be hung again next year in a new arrangement.
picks.best_for: Renters and small spaces with no floor room for a tree
picks.skip_if: Your wall has textured paint or wallpaper, which putty can pull off when removed
picks.quirky_fact: Putty holds light paper for weeks, but heavier cardstock may need a second dab.

faqs.question: What paper works best for Christmas stars?
faqs.answer: Cardstock holds a cut star's points and does not curl, while origami or construction paper is better for folded and woven stars. Use translucent kite or window paper for stars that hang in a window. Avoid thin printer paper for anything that must stand on its own.

faqs.question: How do I make a paper star without glue?
faqs.answer: Fold and weave strips instead. The Froebel star and the woven four-point star both lock together by tucking the strip ends, so no glue or tape is needed. Use stiff, double-sided paper, and pull each fold tight as you go.

faqs.question: Can I put a light inside a paper star lantern?
faqs.answer: Yes, but use a battery LED light, never a bulb that produces heat or a real candle. Paper burns, so a cool LED tea light or a small string of LEDs is the safe choice. Check the lantern's kit instructions for the size of light it holds.

faqs.question: How long does it take to make a paper star?
faqs.answer: A woven four-point star takes about five minutes once you know the fold, a Froebel star about 15, and a 25-point lantern an hour or more. A cut star from a template takes only a minute or two.

faqs.question: How do I store paper stars until next year?
faqs.answer: Keep them flat in a box or folder with tissue paper between layers, away from damp and sun. Folded stars can be nested loosely. Store lanterns folded flat if the design allows, and check that they are fully dry before packing.

answer: The Froebel folded star, the 3D star lantern and the woven four-point star are the best paper stars for Christmas here. Choose by skill level and where it hangs: woven stars suit children, lanterns suit entryways and window stars suit daylight.
method: Picked from Pinterest's trending searches for Christmas paper stars, then chosen for the skill each needs, the cost of materials and where in a home each one can hang.
